newsitem.title: USA: NYC mayor sees plan for Hudson park in 6 months.
newsitem.headline: NYC mayor sees plan for Hudson park in 6 months.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani on Thursday said he anticipated it would take about six months to one year to draft a design plan for a new park proposed along the Hudson River waterfront.

Saying the city had started its push to get the state to approve the park when Mario Cuomo, Gov George Pataki's predecessor, was governor, Giuliani noted the city in 1994 commited $100 million to the effort. "This is a good plan," he told reporters at a news conference on healthcare, saying it gave the city and state a chance to develop what could be a beautiful park. He declined to comment immediately on a controversy over including commercial interests in the park.

New York State Gov George Pataki announced that the state would provide $100 million of funds for the new park, saying it could accommodate a variety of uses. "I am confident that we can develop a world-class maritime park that incorporates public recreation, environmental education, historic and cultural preseration," he said, in prepared remarks.
Giuliani, in a prepared statement, thanked the governor for his support, adding: "The greatest waterfront in the world has been dormant for far too long, inaccessible to city residents."

The state Department of Transportation will transfer its land to the Hudson River Park Conservancy, a unit of New York State's Urban Development Corp, as soon as environmental and legal requirements are met.

The Transportation department also will fully account for revenues paid since 1982 by lease properties located within the planned park, to make certain that the money, once amounts spent on the park are deducted, was spent on the project, as will future rentals, Pataki said. He added a task force will study building a ballfield on Pier 40.

Al Butzel of the Hudson River Park Alliance, who the New York Times said in its Thursday edition had worked on the legal challenge to the Westway riverfront park that was derailed by a host of objections, said he welcomed Pataki's support. So did Paul Elston, chairman of the New York League of Conservation Voters.

But the proposal quickly attracted opposition from at least one environmental group, as the Clean Air Campaign warned in a prepared statement, attacked the mix of private and public interests that would be included, saying that the battle to get an acceptable park was not over.

Saying a state agency and its subsidiary wanted a blank check, it continued: "The state Urban Development Corp and Hudson River Park Conservancy would also have taxpayers subsidize pork-barrel projects in the River, and the money-losing private development that doesn't pay taxes to New York City--in the name of generating illusory 'revenues' to pay for a 'park.'
